config.title: Micro-frontend Shell

intro.title: Micro-frontend Shell
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a micro-frontend shell, which is a React application that acts as a container to host multiple smaller, independent frontend applications. You will learn the core concept of composing a user interface by dynamically loading and rendering different components based on navigation. The main technologies involved are React components, state management with the useState hook, and event handling. By the end, you will have a functional shell that can switch between micro-frontend views, demonstrating a foundational pattern for scalable web development.
intro.usecase: A micro-frontend shell acts as the main container application that dynamically loads and orchestrates multiple, independently developed frontend modules. This pattern is essential in large-scale products like enterprise dashboards, where different teams own separate panels for analytics, user management, or reporting, allowing for independent deployment and updates. It's also used in e-commerce platforms to seamlessly integrate distinct features such as product listings, shopping carts, and recommendation widgets into a single cohesive UI. For developers, this approach enables scalable, maintainable applications by decoupling feature development and reducing cross-team dependencies.

objectives: Construct a React shell component that serves as the main container for micro-frontends
Initialize and manage application state to control which micro-frontend module is displayed
Implement dynamic module loading using React's lazy and Suspense APIs
Configure routing within the shell to handle navigation between different micro-frontend applications
Integrate a navigation component that allows users to switch between micro-frontend modules
Render micro-frontend components conditionally based on the current application state
Apply error boundaries to handle failures when loading micro-frontend modules

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for React and useState are added to the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the MicroFrontendShell component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named MicroFrontendShell that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function with the name MicroFrontendShell and have it return null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the MicroFrontendShell component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A MicroFrontendShell component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The component is named MicroFrontendShell and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named exactly MicroFrontendShell and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check the name and return statement.

steps.title: Initialize state for active micro-frontend
steps.instruction: Inside your MicroFrontendShell component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'activeApp' and initialize it with the string 'dashboard'.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 'dashboard' and destructure the returned array into two variables: activeApp and setActiveApp.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'activeApp' initialized to 'dashboard' and a setter function 'setActiveApp'.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with 'dashboard' as initial value, and the returned array is destructured into 'activeApp' and 'setActiveApp'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with 'dashboard' as the initial value and destructuring the returned array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState('dashboard') inside the component to create the activeApp state variable.

steps.title: Define handler to switch micro-frontends
steps.instruction: Inside the MicroFrontendShell component, create a function named handleAppSwitch that takes an appName parameter and updates the activeApp state with that value.
steps.hint: The function should use the setActiveApp function from useState to update the state. Remember to define it inside your component.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a handleAppSwitch function that can be called to change which micro-frontend is active.
successCriteria: A handleAppSwitch function is defined inside the component, takes an appName parameter, and calls setActiveApp with that parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes an appName parameter and calls setActiveApp with that value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function isn't defined correctly. It should be inside the component, take an appName parameter, and update the state using setActiveApp.

steps.title: Add shell container structure
steps.instruction: In your MicroFrontendShell component, return a div element with the className 'shell-container'.
steps.hint: Replace the current return statement (which returns null) with a div that has the specified class name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div with className 'shell-container' instead of null.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element with className 'shell-container'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a div element with exactly className='shell-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. The component should return a div element with className 'shell-container'.

steps.title: Add navigation header
steps.instruction: Inside the MicroFrontendShell component's return statement, add a <header> element with className 'shell-header' as the first child inside the container div.
steps.hint: The header should be placed directly inside the container div you created earlier. Use JSX syntax: <header className="shell-header"></header>.
steps.expectedOutcome: The shell container now contains a header element with the appropriate class, ready to hold navigation controls.
successCriteria: A <header> element with className 'shell-header' is added as the first child inside the container div.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a header element, but check that it has the correct className 'shell-header' and is placed inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The header element with className 'shell-header' is missing or incorrectly placed. Make sure it's inside the container div in the return statement.

steps.title: Add navigation buttons
steps.instruction: Inside the header element, add three buttons with labels 'Dashboard', 'Analytics', and 'Settings'.
steps.hint: Add the buttons directly inside the header element you created in the previous step. Use the <button> element with appropriate text content.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding navigation buttons inside a header
<header>
  <button>Home</button>
  <button>About</button>
  <button>Contact</button>
</header>
steps.expectedOutcome: The header now contains three buttons labeled 'Dashboard', 'Analytics', and 'Settings'.
successCriteria: Three <button> elements with the correct labels are present inside the header element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have exactly three buttons with the labels 'Dashboard', 'Analytics', and 'Settings' inside the header.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigation buttons are missing or incorrect. Please add three <button> elements with the specified labels inside the header.

steps.title: Wire buttons to switch handler
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to each button that calls handleAppSwitch with the appropriate app name ('dashboard', 'profile', or 'settings').
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on each button to call handleAppSwitch with the correct string argument.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: wiring a button to a handler
<button onClick={() => handleClick('home')}>Home</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Each button will have an onClick handler that calls handleAppSwitch with the correct app name.
successCriteria: All three buttons have onClick handlers that call handleAppSwitch with the appropriate arguments.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Some buttons are wired correctly, but others are missing onClick handlers or have incorrect arguments.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are not wired to the handler. Make sure each button has an onClick that calls handleAppSwitch with the correct app name.

steps.title: Add content area for micro-frontends
steps.instruction: Add a main element with className 'shell-content' after the header in your component's return statement.
steps.hint: Place the <main> element directly after the closing </header> tag. Use the className attribute to set the CSS class.
steps.expectedOutcome: The shell container will have a main content area ready to display micro-frontend content.
successCriteria: A <main> element with className='shell-content' is added after the header.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a <main> element with className='shell-content' after the header.
steps.feedbackWrong: The content area is missing. Add a <main> element with className='shell-content' after the header.

steps.title: Display active micro-frontend content
steps.instruction: Inside the content area, use conditional rendering to show different content based on the activeApp state. Display a heading and paragraph for each micro-frontend (dashboard, profile, settings).
steps.hint: You can use a ternary operator or if-else logic inside JSX to conditionally render content based on the activeApp value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The shell will display different content sections when you click the navigation buttons, showing the currently active micro-frontend.
successCriteria: Conditional rendering is implemented to display different content for dashboard, profile, and settings based on the activeApp state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying distinct content for each micro-frontend (dashboard, profile, settings) based on the activeApp value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The content area should show different content for each micro-frontend based on the activeApp state. Try using conditional rendering with the activeApp variable.
